comparisons.peer_topic: R&D Expense Increase and AI Headcount
comparisons.peer_summary: AMD's research and development expenses increased by 10% to $6.5 billion in 2024, primarily driven by higher employee-related costs resulting from an increase in headcount to support the company's AI strategy.
comparisons.comparison: Like NVDA, AMD attributed its R&D expense increases in FY 2024 primarily to higher employee-related costs and headcount growth. NVDA stated the increase was driven by compensation and benefits reflecting employee growth, while AMD noted the increase was due to higher employee-related costs from an increase in headcount specifically to support its AI strategy.

sentences.text: The increase in research and development expenses and sales, general and administrative expenses for fiscal year 2024 was primarily driven by compensation and benefits, including stock-based compensation, reflecting employee growth and compensation increases.
The increase was primarily due to higher employee-related costs due to an increase in headcount in support of our AI strategy.

comparisons.peer_summary: Marketing, general and administrative expenses were $2.8 billion in 2024, an increase of $431 million or 18% from $2.4 billion in 2023, primarily due to increased go-to-market activities supporting revenue growth.
comparisons.comparison: Similar to NVDA's driver of SG&A increases via compensation and employee growth, AMD's SG&A (Marketing, general and administrative) expenses increased primarily due to increased go-to-market activities. While NVDA explicitly cited compensation/employee growth as the driver for both R&D and SG&A, AMD cited go-to-market activities, though both reflect expansionary spending to support revenue.

comparisons.comparison: AVGO's R&D expense increase was primarily driven by higher compensation and headcount, mirroring NVDA's primary driver of compensation and benefits reflecting employee growth. AVGO further specified that the headcount increase resulted from the VMware Merger and that stock-based compensation was higher due to higher grant-date fair values, a detail NVDA also explicitly included in its disclosure.
